formation.title: The New World
formation.text:
No crown from beyond the ocean holds American soil any longer. The lands of the Americas are ruled from within them, and most of them from one capital.

Two plans for such a power were drawn before it existed. In 1790 Francisco de Miranda proposed a single great state from the Mississippi to Cape Horn, under one hereditary head with a senate for life and an elected chamber. In 1826 Bolivar's congress at Panama drafted a treaty of union, league and perpetual confederation: free states bound to defend one another and to settle their quarrels in peace.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: One great state from the Mississippi to Cape Horn.

modifiers.name: The Great State
modifiers.text: One government rules the Americas from the Mississippi to Cape Horn.

options.text: A perpetual confederation of American states.

modifiers.name: The Perpetual Confederation
modifiers.text: The American states are bound to defend one another and to settle their quarrels in peace.

advances.name: Palenques and Quilombos
advances.text: Wherever the plantations of the Americas stood, the enslaved fled them for the forest and the mountain and built free towns there: the palenques of New Granada, the quilombos of Brazil, the Maroon towns of Jamaica and Suriname. Palmares held out in the hills of Pernambuco for most of the seventeenth century, and in 1713 the crown of Spain gave up its campaigns against San Basilio de Palenque and recognised it as free.

event.title: The Free Towns of the Mountains
event.text: For a century the colonial powers sent columns into the hills after the free towns of escaped slaves, and the columns came back thinned by fever and ambush. Two ways of ending these wars were found. In 1713 Spain recognised San Basilio de Palenque as a free town and left it alone. In 1739, under a cotton tree in Jamaica, Cudjoe's Maroons signed a treaty that gave them their freedom and their land, and bound them in return to guard the colony's frontier and hunt down later runaways.

options.text: Recognise the free towns by charter.

modifiers.name: Charters of the Free Towns
modifiers.text: The free towns of the hills are recognised and hold the frontier as strongholds.

options.text: Enlist the Maroons as rangers of the frontier.

modifiers.name: Maroon Frontier Companies
modifiers.text: Maroon companies guide our columns and harry any enemy in the forests.

advances.name: The Royal Roads
advances.text: The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro ran more than two thousand kilometres from Mexico City to Santa Fe, and in January 1673 the first regular post rider set out from New York for Boston on the road that became the Boston Post Road. Along such roads the posts kept relays of horses and riders, and the news of one end of a continent reached the other in weeks instead of seasons.

advances.name: The Fever Bark
advances.text: The bark of the cinchona, a tree of the Andean forests around Loja, cured the fevers of the tropics. Jesuits carried it to Rome in the 1640s, the London Pharmacopoeia listed it as Peruvian bark in 1677, and the bark gatherers of the Andes, the cascarilleros, stripped it for the markets of the world.

advances.name: The Thirty Towns
advances.text: The Guarani of the Jesuit missions between the Parana and the Uruguay lived in towns of their own, with their own officers and their own militia. Armed by leave of the crown in 1640, they met the slave raiders of Sao Paulo on the Uruguay river at Mborore on 11 March 1641 and broke them; the mission militias stood guard on that frontier for over a century.

advances.name: The Gazettes of the Indies
advances.text: Sigüenza y Góngora's Mercurio Volante was printed in Mexico in 1693, the Boston News-Letter began in 1704, and the Gaceta de México in January 1722. Read aloud in taverns and copied from port to port, the American gazettes carried the news of one province to the next.

advances.name: The General Languages
advances.text: Nahuatl, Quechua, Guarani and the Tupi of the Brazilian lingua geral spread far beyond their homelands as the common tongues of mission, market and road. Priests preached in them, officials governed in them, and peoples who shared no other language traded in them.

advances.name: The Rising of Saint-Domingue
advances.text: In August 1791 the enslaved of the northern plain of Saint-Domingue rose. Thirteen years later, after Toussaint Louverture had made the colony his and Dessalines had beaten the army Napoleon sent to take it back, Haiti declared its independence on 1 January 1804: the second free state of the Americas, and the first made by the enslaved themselves.

event.title: Two Republics of Haiti
event.text: Independence did not settle what Haiti would be. In the north Henri Christophe, king from 1811, kept the plantations at work by forced labour and raised the Citadelle on a mountain above Milot against the return of the French. In the south Alexandre Pétion's republic divided the state's land, from 1809, into small plots for its soldiers and then for anyone who could buy one; the smallholders grew food, and the sugar exports of the old colony withered.

options.text: Raise the citadels and keep the fields at work.

modifiers.name: Citadel of the North
modifiers.text: Mountain fortresses guard the country, built and fed by labour on the old plantations.

options.text: Divide the plantations among the cultivators.

modifiers.name: Land of the Cultivators
modifiers.text: The great estates are divided into smallholdings that feed their owners rather than the export trade.

advances.name: The Pledge of Les Cayes
advances.text: In 1816 Simón Bolívar, beaten and in exile, came to Haiti. President Alexandre Pétion gave him muskets, powder, ships and money for one promise: freedom for the enslaved of every land he liberated. Bolívar's decrees of Carúpano and Ocumare followed that year, and the congress of Cúcuta made every child born to an enslaved mother free in 1821.

event.title: The Promise Kept
event.text: Pétion asked for one thing in return for his muskets: freedom for the enslaved. At Carúpano on 2 June 1816 Bolívar declared free every slave who took up arms for the republic, and at Ocumare a month later every slave without condition. Freedom came to many with a musket, and the armies of independence filled with freedmen. Others asked what freedom was worth without land to live on, as Haiti's smallholders had answered.

options.text: Freedom for every man who takes up arms.

modifiers.name: Freedom under Arms
modifiers.text: The freedmen fill the ranks of the armies that freed them.

options.text: Freedom, and land to work.

modifiers.name: Freedom on the Land
modifiers.text: The freed are given land, and with it a living of their own.

advances.name: The Llaneros
advances.text: The horsemen of the Orinoco plains fought first for the king and then, under José Antonio Páez, for the republic. On 2 April 1819 at Las Queseras del Medio some 150 of them swam the Arauca, drew Morillo's cavalry after them and turned on it with the lance.

advances.name: The Army of the Andes
advances.text: José de San Martín raised and drilled his army for two years at Mendoza. In January 1817 it went over the Andes in two columns, by the passes of Los Patos and Uspallata, and on 12 February it broke the royalists at Chacabuco and opened the road to Santiago.

event.title: Over the Andes
event.text: The Army of the Andes came down into Chile in February 1817 and broke the royalists at Chacabuco. The road to the last royal stronghold, Lima, lay either by sea, as San Martín sailed from Valparaíso in 1820 with Cochrane's squadron, or over the mountains, as Bolívar had led his army across the frozen Páramo de Pisba in 1819 to fall on New Granada from behind.

options.text: North by sea.

modifiers.name: The Liberating Expedition
modifiers.text: The army goes north by sea under the escort of the squadron.

options.text: North over the mountains.

modifiers.name: The Road over the Andes
modifiers.text: The army goes north through the high passes, where no enemy expects it.

advances.name: The Patriot Militias
advances.text: The wars that ended the crowns' rule in the Americas were fought less by regular armies than by militias raised in town and countryside: farmers, artisans, freedmen and herdsmen who called themselves patriots from Boston to Buenos Aires.

advances.name: The Squadron of the Pacific
advances.text: The independence of the Pacific coast was won at sea as much as on land. Chile's squadron under Thomas Cochrane stormed the forts of Valdivia in February 1820 and, on the night of 5 November 1820, rowed into Callao under the guns of its forts and cut out the frigate Esmeralda.

advances.name: The Botanical Expeditions
advances.text: From 1783 José Celestino Mutis's Royal Botanical Expedition catalogued the plants of New Granada and painted thousands of plates, and in 1803 he had an observatory built in its garden at Santa Fe de Bogotá. Humboldt passed through on his journey of 1799 to 1804, and the scientists of the expedition, Caldas among them, became the learned men of the independence.

advances.name: Steam on the Rivers
advances.text: In 1811 the steamboat New Orleans left Pittsburgh and went down the Ohio and the Mississippi to the city it was named for. In 1823 the congress of Colombia gave Juan Bernardo Elbers the privilege of steam navigation on the Magdalena. The great rivers of the Americas became roads that ran both ways.

destiny.name: The Destiny of the New World
destiny.text: No crown from beyond the ocean rules in the Americas any longer. What the New World does with its power is still to be settled: carry it over the oceans as one great state, or bind the states of the hemisphere into a league.

event.title: The Hemisphere's Own
event.text: The last royal governor has sailed for home, and the Americas are ruled from within them. Two plans for what comes next were written before the crowns left: Miranda's single great state, and the league of free states that Bolívar called to Panama.

options.text: The New World will choose its own course.

destiny.name: The Galleon Road
destiny.text: For two and a half centuries the Manila galleon crossed the Pacific between Acapulco and Manila, and the Philippines were governed through Mexico City; the westbound ships put in at Guam for water. When the galleons stopped in 1815, the islands were left to a crown on the far side of the world. Maynila and Guahan must be held, and 30,000 men kept under arms.

conditions.text: Own Maynila, or a subject owns it
Own Guahan, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Galleon Road
event.text: The flag of the New World flies over Manila and over the watering place at Guam. In June 1823 Andrés Novales, a Manila-born officer angry that the crown was replacing the officers born in the Indies with men sent from Spain, had seized the walled city and been hailed emperor for a single day. What he could not hold has now been taken from the American side of the ocean.

options.text: The Pacific is an American sea.

destiny.name: The Fortunate Isles
destiny.text: The Canaries were the last port of call of every fleet bound for the Indies, and their families settled Caracas, Havana and the bayous of Louisiana. Francisco de Miranda's father was born at Puerto de la Cruz, in the valley of La Orotava on Tenerife. Aguere on Tenerife and Tamaraceite on Gran Canaria must be held, with 2,000 gold in the treasury and 50 prestige.

conditions.text: Own Aguere, or a subject owns it
Own Tamaraceite, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Fortunate Isles
event.text: Tenerife and Gran Canaria are held. For three centuries every fleet bound for the Indies took its last water here, and the islanders followed the fleets to Caracas, Havana and Louisiana. Now the islands must be given a purpose: a station for the fleet that guards the Atlantic road, or a port open to the ships of every nation.

options.text: Make the islands the fleet's station.

modifiers.name: The Atlantic Station
modifiers.text: The fleet that guards the Atlantic road is based, victualled and repaired in the Canaries.

options.text: Open the islands to every flag.

modifiers.name: The Free Port of the Islands
modifiers.text: The Canaries are open to the ships of every nation, and their customs are given up.

destiny.name: The Ports of the Indies
destiny.text: Seville held the monopoly of the Indies trade until 1717, when the Casa de Contratación moved to Cádiz. At Cádiz the Cortes of 1810 to 1812 refused the American deputies a share of the seats by their numbers. The great state now answers from the other shore. Cádiz and Sevilla must be held, with 75,000 men under arms and 75 prestige.

conditions.text: Own Cádiz, or a subject owns it
Own Sevilla, or a subject owns it

event.title: Cádiz and Seville
event.text: The ports that once held the monopoly of the Indies trade are held from the far shore of the ocean. In 1812 the Cortes at Cádiz had written a constitution for the Spaniards of both hemispheres, yet would not seat the Americans by their numbers. The great state can do what the Cortes would not, or it can keep the city as the fortress that the French besieged for two years and never took.

options.text: Seat both shores in one assembly.

modifiers.name: The Cortes of Both Shores
modifiers.text: One assembly seats the peoples of both shores of the ocean by their numbers.

options.text: Hold Cádiz as a fortress.

modifiers.name: The Bulwark of Cádiz
modifiers.text: Cádiz is kept as a fortress, and the money goes to its walls and garrison instead of new works.

destiny.name: The Congress of Panama
destiny.text: From 22 June to 15 July 1826 the envoys of Gran Colombia, Peru, Mexico and Central America met in the chapter house of the convent of San Francisco in Panama and signed a treaty of union, league and perpetual confederation. Panama must grow into a city, held by the New World or one of its subjects; three loyal subjects with their capitals in the Americas must stand in the confederation; and 1,000 gold must be in the treasury.

conditions.text: Panama is a City or larger, held by us or one of our subjects
At least 3 loyal subjects have their capital in the Americas

event.title: The Amphictyony of Panama
event.text: Bolívar wished that the isthmus might be to the Americans what Corinth had been to the Greeks, and called his congress there the Amphictyony. Panama has grown into a city, and the states of the confederation govern themselves under the league. What failed in 1826 has been made to stand.

options.text: Let each state keep its own counsel.

destiny.name: The League of Common Defence
destiny.text: The treaty of Panama bound its members to defend one another and to settle their quarrels in peace, and a convention of contingents set the troops each would keep. Only Gran Colombia ratified it, and the assembly that was to meet again at Tacubaya never sat. A defensive league of at least four countries with their capitals in the Americas is needed, with 50,000 men under arms and 50 prestige.

conditions.text: We are in a Defensive League with at least 4 members whose capital is in the Americas, ourselves included

event.title: The League of Common Defence
event.text: The free states of the Americas are bound to defend one another. The treaty of 1826 asked two things of its members: troops for the common army, set state by state in the convention of contingents, and the settlement of their quarrels in peace. The league must now choose which it will be known by.

options.text: Each state keeps its quota of troops.

modifiers.name: The Quotas of Contingents
modifiers.text: Every state of the league keeps the troops the common defence asks of it.

options.text: Settle every quarrel by arbitration.

modifiers.name: Arbitration of Disputes
modifiers.text: Quarrels between the states are put to the assembly instead of to arms, and the armies are neglected.

destiny.name: The Emporium of the Universe
destiny.text: Writing from Jamaica in 1815, Bolívar foresaw that the isthmus, set between two great seas, might in time become the emporium of the universe, its canals shortening the distances of the world and binding the trade of Europe, America and Asia. Panama must be a market centre that trades porcelain, held by the New World or one of its subjects, with 3,000 gold in the treasury and 75 prestige.

conditions.text: Panama is a Market Center that trades Porcelain, held by us or one of our subjects

event.title: The Emporium of the Universe
event.text: The goods of China are sold on the isthmus, and the ships of both oceans call at Panama. In the days of the fleets the silver of Peru crossed it on mule trains by the Camino de Cruces and the Chagres river. Panama can become a free port where the trade of three continents changes hands, or the road across the isthmus can be made the shortest way between the oceans.

options.text: Make the isthmus a free port.

modifiers.name: The Free Port of the Isthmus
modifiers.text: The goods of Europe, America and Asia change hands at Panama free of duty.

options.text: Build the road between the oceans.

modifiers.name: The Road between the Oceans
modifiers.text: A road across the isthmus carries goods from one ocean to the other in days.

units.name: Maroon Rangers
units.text: Fighters of the free towns of the forest and mountain, at home in country that starves the columns sent against them.

units.name: Demi-Brigade of the Armée Indigène
units.text: The line infantry of the army that held Crête-à-Pierrot and won at Vertières, hardened to a climate that destroyed its enemies.

units.name: Llanero Lancers
units.text: Horsemen of the plains with lance and no armour, who swim rivers on horseback and turn on their pursuers.

units.name: Mounted Grenadiers
units.text: The heavy horse San Martín raised in 1812, which crossed the Andes and rode from San Lorenzo to Ayacucho.

units.name: Squadron Frigate
units.text: A fast, well gunned frigate of the squadrons the American republics raised on the Pacific.

units.name: Patriot Militia
units.text: Farmers, artisans and freedmen under arms for their country.

buildings.name: Post House
buildings.text: A relay station on a royal road: fresh horses, a rider and the mail.

buildings.name: Cascarilla Camp
buildings.text: A camp of bark gatherers in the montane forest, where the cinchona bark is stripped, dried and packed for the coast, and more of the forest's bark reaches the market. It can stand only where the land yields medicinal plants.

where.text: The location's raw material is Medicaments

buildings.name: Astronomical Observatory
buildings.text: An observatory for the measure of the sky and of the land, where the longitudes of a continent are fixed.

effect_groups.label: To the country, when built in the capital

buildings.name: Steamboat Landing
buildings.text: A wharf, woodyard and warehouse where the river steamers call.

list.name: Open Cabildos
list.text: In an emergency the town council is summoned open to all the leading householders of the city. So were the royal officials deposed at Caracas on 19 April 1810 and at Buenos Aires in May, and juntas named in their place, on the doctrine that sovereignty returns to the people while the king is a prisoner.

list.name: Tribunals of the Consulado
list.text: The merchants judge their own disputes and spend a duty on imports, the averia, on roads and ports. Mexico has had its consulado since 1592 and Lima since 1613; more were founded from 1793 to 1795, Buenos Aires and Veracruz among them, and the one at Veracruz built the carriage road by Xalapa to Perote. At Buenos Aires its secretary Manuel Belgrano wrote each year against the monopolists of the port.

list.name: Schools of Mutual Instruction
list.text: One master teaches the monitors, and the monitors teach the rest, by Joseph Lancaster's method. It was brought to Buenos Aires in 1818, a company was founded at Mexico in 1822 to spread it, and the congress of Cucuta ordered a school in every town of a hundred families. In 1824 Colombia counted 52 such schools against 434 kept by the clergy.

list.name: Vaccine Boards
list.text: Boards of vaccine were founded in the chief cities as the royal expedition of Francisco Javier de Balmis passed in 1804; at Caracas the young Andres Bello was secretary of the first. A conservator keeps the cowpox alive from arm to arm, and the parishes record those vaccinated.

list.name: Lighthorse Companies
list.text: Mounted companies ride against horse thieves and carry the nation's written law where clan revenge once ruled. The Cherokee formed regulating companies in 1795 and set the lighthorse under their law of 1808; the Choctaw raised theirs in 1824, and the Chickasaw a hundred riders in 1829.

list.name: Patriot Privateers
list.text: Letters of marque against Spanish shipping are sold to any captain who will fit out a ship. Buenos Aires and Artigas issued most of them from 1816, Mexico and Colombia after 1821, and more than a hundred ships out of the United States, most from Baltimore, sailed under the patriot flags.
